title: IVF-PQ: billion scale on one machine
summary: Encoding the residual from the cell centroid rather than the raw vector is the idea that makes IVF-PQ work, and its value scales with how good your coarse quantizer is: measured, the gain triples going from 16 cells to 1024. The result is a billion vectors resident in 32 GB with the full data on SSD.
html:
Day 20 solved which vectors to look at. Days 21 and 22 solved how expensive each one is to look at. Today they combine, and the result is the configuration that puts a billion vectors on a single machine.

The naive combination is what you would guess: cluster into cells, PQ-encode the vectors, scan the codes in the probed cells with ADC. That works. The version everyone actually ships has one extra idea in it, and it is the part most explanations skip.

Encode the residual, not the vector

After the coarse quantizer runs, you already know roughly where a vector is: it is near centroid c. So spending your 24 bytes describing its absolute position wastes most of them re-encoding information the cell id already carries.

Encode the residual instead, the offset from the centroid:

r = x - centroid(x)

store:  cell id  +  PQ code of r

Residuals are smaller and less spread out than raw vectors, so the same 256 centroids per subspace cover them at finer resolution. The coarse quantizer handles the gross position, PQ handles the local correction, and neither duplicates the other's work.

Scoring still decomposes cleanly. Since x is approximately c + r:

q . x  ~  q . c  +  q . r

         per-cell constant     ADC table sum over the residual code
         computed once per     m lookups and m adds, exactly as Day 22
         probed cell

One extra float add per candidate, and the per-cell term is amortised across every vector in that list.

Does it help? It depends on your coarse quantizer

I measured it both ways on the 6,200 document embeddings, 24 bytes per vector either way:

nlist  residual norm  vs raw   raw-PQ  residual-PQ    gain
   16         0.9040     90%    0.557        0.591  +0.034
   64         0.8615     86%    0.617        0.634  +0.017
  256         0.8046     80%    0.625        0.644  +0.019
 1024         0.6906     69%    0.628        0.678  +0.050

The mechanism is in the second column. With 16 cells the centroids are poor summaries, so the residual is still 90 percent as big as the original vector and encoding it buys little. With 1,024 cells the centroids are close to their members, residuals shrink to 69 percent, and the gain triples.

So residual encoding is not a free trick you bolt on. Its value is a function of how good your coarse quantizer is, and the two components are coupled: more cells make both the search cheaper and the compression better. At a billion vectors with 31,000 cells, residuals are far smaller than anything I can show at this scale, and the gain is correspondingly larger.

Be sceptical of my absolute numbers here. 6,200 vectors is a weak test: 24 training points per PQ centroid (Day 21's caveat) and cells holding a handful of vectors each at nlist=1024. The trend across the table is the finding, not the values.

One set of codebooks, not one per cell

An obvious refinement suggests itself: residuals in different cells have different distributions, so why not train separate PQ codebooks per cell? More accurate, surely.

Price it before you build it. At a billion vectors with 31,622 cells:

shared codebooks     0.393 MB     one set, trained on residuals from everywhere
per-cell codebooks   12.4 GB      31,622 copies of the same structure

You would spend more on codebooks than on the codes they decode, and each one would be trained on a thirty-thousandth of the data. Shared codebooks win on both counts, which is why residual encoding matters so much: it is what makes one global codebook reasonable across cells that sit in completely different parts of the space. Subtract the centroid and residuals from everywhere start to look alike.

Training, which is a sampling problem

You do not run k-means on a billion vectors. You sample, fit the quantizers on the sample, then encode everything in one streaming pass.

How large a sample follows from the hundred-points-per-centroid guidance in Day 21:

coarse quantizer, 31,622 centroids  ->  about 3.2M training vectors
PQ, 256 centroids per subspace      ->  about  26K training vectors

So a few million sampled vectors trains the whole index, and the encoding pass over the remaining billion is embarrassingly parallel and streams straight through. Build cost is dominated by the encode, not the fit, which is the opposite of what people expect and good news for rebuilds.

The full query path

1. score query against nlist centroids            -> pick nprobe cells
2. build the m x 256 ADC table                    -> once per query
3. for each probed cell:
      scan its codes, m lookups + m adds each
      add the per-cell q.c constant
4. keep the top few hundred by approximate score
5. fetch those full vectors from SSD, rescore exactly
6. return top k

Steps 1 to 4 run entirely in memory on compressed data. Step 5 is the only thing that touches the real vectors, and it touches a few hundred of them.

The budget, at a billion

PQ codes          24.0 GB     24 bytes x 1e9
vector ids         8.0 GB     8 bytes x 1e9
coarse centroids   0.049 GB   31,622 x 384 floats
PQ codebooks       0.393 MB   shared, fixed size
-------------------------------------------
resident total    32.0 GB

full vectors       1.54 TB    on SSD, read only for rescoring

Thirty two gigabytes. A billion vectors fits in the RAM of one ordinary server, and the terabyte and a half of real data sits on disk where it belongs.

Note the ids line. Eight bytes per vector for an int64 is a third of what the codes cost, and if your corpus fits in four billion you should be using int32 and saving 4 GB. That is the kind of detail that is invisible in a paper and obvious in a capacity plan.

Per query, at nprobe=32:

candidates scanned    1,011,954   (0.1% of the corpus)
bytes read from RAM        24.3 MB  (vs 1,554 MB uncompressed)
rescore from SSD            150 KB  in ~100 random reads

Twenty four megabytes of sequential reads through cache-resident lookup tables, then a hundred small random reads from flash. Both halves are doing the thing their storage medium is good at, which is the whole argument for this architecture over a graph.

What you give up

Recall, mostly in the first stage. Everything above is approximate twice over: IVF can route past the right cell (Day 20's boundary problem) and PQ can mis-rank within a cell. The rescoring pass fixes ordering errors but cannot recover a vector that was never in the shortlist, so your ceiling is set by stages 1 to 4 and nothing downstream repairs it.

The practical consequence is that you tune nprobe and the shortlist size together against recall, not separately. A bigger shortlist is cheap, more probes are not, and if recall is short the answer is almost always more probes rather than more rescoring.

One thing has been quietly wrong since Day 21. I split the 384 dimensions into contiguous blocks of 16, which assumes adjacent dimensions belong together. In a learned embedding they do not, and some blocks end up carrying far more variance than others. Tomorrow fixes that with a learned rotation: OPQ.
exercise:
1. Measure your own residual shrinkage. Cluster your vectors into sqrt(N) cells, compute the mean norm of x - centroid(x), and divide by the mean norm of x. That ratio predicts how much residual encoding will buy you. Below about 0.9 it is worth doing, near 1.0 your coarse quantizer is too coarse to help.

2. Build your own budget table. For your real corpus size and dimension, compute PQ codes, ids, centroids and codebooks at m=16, 24 and 48, and total them. Compare against the machine you would actually deploy on. Check whether your ids should be int32.

3. Find where your recall is lost. Run your index at a fixed shortlist size and sweep nprobe, then fix nprobe and sweep the shortlist. One of those curves will be flat. The flat one is not your bottleneck, and knowing which is which saves you tuning the wrong knob for a week.
